sentences: Yes, but only as an exception.
The normal daily limit is 9 hours of driving.
You may extend it to at most 10 hours, but no more than twice in the same week (Monday 00.00 to Sunday 24.00).
The 10-hour day still counts towards your other limits: no more than 56 hours of driving in the week and no more than 90 hours in any two consecutive weeks.
Daily driving time is all driving between the end of one daily rest and the start of the next daily or weekly rest.

There is also a separate emergency exception, for exceptional circumstances and only if road safety is not put at risk: you may exceed the daily limit by up to 1 hour to get to your employer's operational centre or your home for a weekly rest.
This becomes up to 2 hours if you take an uninterrupted 30-minute break just before the extra driving and go home for a regular weekly rest.
You must write the reason by hand on the record sheet, printout or duty roster, and make up the extra time with equivalent rest by the end of the third week after.

sentences: Your next weekly rest must start no later than the end of six 24-hour periods (144 hours) after your previous weekly rest ended.
Exception: a driver on a single occasional passenger service (coach trip) may postpone the weekly rest for up to 12 consecutive 24-hour periods after a previous regular weekly rest.

Afterwards the driver must take either two regular weekly rests, or one regular and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours, with the reduction made up en bloc before the end of the third week after the derogation period.
The vehicle also needs the required recording equipment, and for driving between 22:00 and 06:00 the vehicle must be multi-manned or the driving period is cut to three hours.

Commission guidance note 4, an older note from March 2015 written before the 2020 Mobility Package, lets enforcement officers allow a tolerance of up to 15 minutes per 4.5-hour block of driving.
This can be applied, for example, as a deduction of one minute for each driving block between stops.
Conditions:
- It is a transitional tolerance.
It covers only vehicles whose digital tachographs were activated before October 2011 and do not meet Regulation 1266/2009.
Newer tachographs already record multi-drop work more accurately.
- The trip must clearly involve frequent or multi-drop stops.
- You must be able to back the claim with evidence, such as proof of the drops.

sentences: Periods of availability are times that are not breaks or rest, when you do not have to stay at your workstation but must be ready to answer calls to start or resume driving or to do other work.
They include accompanying a vehicle carried by ferry or train, waiting at frontiers, and waiting because of traffic bans.

sentences: Under Directive 2002/15/EC you count as a 'self-employed driver' only if you meet all of these conditions:
- Your main occupation is carrying passengers or goods by road for hire or reward, under a Community licence or another professional authorisation.
- You are entitled to work for yourself.
- You are not tied to an employer by an employment contract or any other working hierarchical relationship.
- You are free to organise your own working activities.
- Your income depends directly on the profits made.
- You are free to have commercial relations with several customers, on your own or through cooperation with other self-employed drivers.
A driver who does not meet these criteria has the same obligations and rights as an employed mobile worker under the Directive.
The Directive has applied to self-employed drivers since 23 March 2009.

sentences: A 30-hour weekly rest counts as a reduced weekly rest, because it is at least 24 hours but shorter than a regular one.
You must make up the missing hours as one equivalent block of rest (not split up), taken before the end of the third week after the week in which you took the reduced rest.
That compensation rest must be attached to another rest period of at least 9 hours, such as a daily or weekly rest.
If this makes a weekly rest of more than 45 hours, you may not spend it in the vehicle.
It must be in suitable accommodation with proper sleeping and sanitary facilities, and your employer pays for it.
If you took two reduced weekly rests in a row (allowed in international goods transport), the compensation for both must come immediately before your next weekly rest.

But if you also drive routes that are in scope, you must keep tachograph records for all your driving, whichever type you do most.

sentences: Yes.
A daily rest period may be extended so that it becomes a regular weekly rest period or a reduced weekly rest period.
A regular weekly rest is at least 45 hours.
A reduced weekly rest is less than 45 hours but at least 24 consecutive hours, and only under the Article 8(6) conditions.
Those conditions are: in any two consecutive weeks you must take at least two regular weekly rests, or one regular and one reduced weekly rest of at least 24 hours.
Your weekly rest must start no later than at the end of six 24-hour periods after your previous weekly rest.
Any reduction of a weekly rest must be made up as one block of rest before the end of the third week after the week in question.
Two more points: a regular weekly rest may not be taken in the vehicle, and neither may a weekly rest of more than 45 hours taken as compensation.

Today the EU driving time rules cover goods vehicles over 3,5 tonnes, so a 3-tonne van is outside them.
From 1 July 2026 the rules also apply to international and cabotage goods transport in vehicles over 2,5 tonnes.
The weight includes any trailer.
From that date your cross-border 3-tonne vans will be covered.
There is one exemption for vans between 2,5 and 3,5 tonnes.
It applies only when the transport is not for hire or reward but on the own account of the company or driver, and driving is not the driver's main activity.
If you deliver for customers for payment, or your staff are mainly drivers, the exemption does not help you.

sentences.reason: The claim that the rules do not apply now but will later follows from Article 2(1)(a), which sets the current 3,5-tonne threshold, and Article 2(1)(aa), which adds vehicles over 2,5 tonnes from 1 July 2026.
Article 2(1)(a) applies the Regulation to goods carriage where the vehicle's maximum permissible mass exceeds 3,5 tonnes, so a 3-tonne van falls below it.
Article 2(1)(aa) extends the rules from 1 July 2026 to international and cabotage goods transport in vehicles exceeding 2,5 tonnes.
Both Article 2(1)(a) and (aa) state that the maximum permissible mass is measured 'including any trailer, or semi-trailer'.
Under Article 2(1)(aa), cross-border goods transport in vehicles over 2,5 tonnes is covered from 1 July 2026, which includes 3-tonne vans.
Article 3(ha) sets out an exemption for goods vehicles exceeding 2,5 tonnes but not exceeding 3,5 tonnes.
Article 3(ha) limits the exemption to transport not effected for hire or reward but on the own account of the company or driver, where driving is not the driver's main activity.
It follows from the conditions in Article 3(ha) that hire-or-reward deliveries, or drivers whose main activity is driving, fall outside the exemption.

sentences: Yes.
Since 2 February 2022 you must enter the symbol of the country you enter after crossing a border of a Member State.
Do this at the start of your first stop in that country, and make that stop at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border.
If you cross the border on a ferry or train, enter the country symbol at the port or station of arrival.
You must also always enter the country symbols where your daily working period starts and finishes.
You may take your driver card out to enter the country symbol after crossing a border.

You don't have to enter the start and end country symbols if the tachograph records location data automatically under Article 8; the passage states this exemption only for those start and end entries.

sentences.reason: The affirmative answer that a border-crossing entry is required is backed by Article 34(7), second subparagraph, which obliges the driver to enter the country symbol after crossing a Member State border.
Article 34(7) states that from 2 February 2022 the driver shall enter the symbol of the country entered after crossing a Member State border.
Article 34(7) requires the entry at the beginning of the first stop in that Member State, made at the nearest possible stopping place at or after the border.
Article 34(7) provides that for a crossing on a ferry or train the symbol is entered at the port or station of arrival.

Article 34(7) requires entry of the start and finish country symbols, but its last subparagraph exempts drivers when the tachograph records location automatically, so the claim that this must 'always' be done contradicts the cited text.
Article 34(1) permits withdrawal of the driver card where it is necessary to enter the country symbol after crossing a border.
Article 34(7)'s last subparagraph removes only the first-subparagraph (start and finish) entries when location data is recorded automatically under Article 8, matching the sentence's scope.
